title: CONGENITAL MYOPATHY 10B, MILD VARIANT
alt_titles: MYOPATHY, AREFLEXIA, RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, AND DYSPHAGIA, EARLY-ONSET, MILD VARIANT

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that the mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene on chromosome 5.

checks.claim: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected subjects were compound heterozygous for missense mutations c.976T > C (p.C326R) and c.2320T > C (p.C774R).
checks.explanation: Paper reports compound heterozygous mutations only; no homozygous mutation.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 gene is located on chromosome 5.
checks.evidence_quote: MEGF10 lies within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329.

paragraphs.text: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10 (CMYO10B) is an autosomal recessive myopathy. Its onset ranges from infancy or childhood to adulthood. Features include predominantly axial and proximal muscle weakness, facial weakness, scoliosis, joint contractures, palatal abnormalities with hypernasal speech, dysphagia, and respiratory insufficiency that develops later in the disease course. Muscle biopsy can show a mixture of dystrophic and myopathic changes, including minicores, and myofibrillar alterations have also been described (Boyden et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2018; Croci et al., 2022). The disorder is milder than the severe early-onset form of MEGF10-related myopathy, which is characterized by areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (Takayama et al., 2016; Croci et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) studied a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an unclassified autosomal recessive myopathy. Weakness appeared by 12 months of age, starting in the neck. It involved the whole body but was mainly axial and proximal, and it stabilized in adolescence. Facial weakness was also present. Neck contractures were seen in infancy, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords had developed by adulthood. Serum creatine kinase measured before age 10 years was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis that was treated with spinal fusion. From age 10 to 11 years, all developed respiratory problems that were treated with nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation. One patient was born with a cleft palate, a second had a midline palatal ridge in adulthood, and the third had a normal-appearing palate. All 3 affected sibs had hypernasal speech. Muscle biopsies showed replacement of myofibers by fatty tissue, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers, which are features of muscular dystrophy. However, the biopsies also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, suggesting a congenital myopathy. Most atrophic fibers were type I, most hypertrophic fibers were type II, and type I fibers slightly predominated. Before genetic testing, the diagnosis had been given as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy or spinal muscular atrophy.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also reported a Caucasian woman of distant Portuguese ancestry (subject 105-1) who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease and who had no affected relatives. Hypotonia appeared at several weeks of age, initially as a weak neck and floppy head. She had a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. As a child she had frequent acute pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. At age 10 years, serum creatine kinase was mildly elevated at 302 U/L, and the mild scoliosis noted at that time had progressed to 20 degrees by age 12. She had mild, nonprogressive, mainly proximal weakness, including facial weakness. Muscle biopsy showed marked variation in fiber size, internalized nuclei, slightly increased endomysial connective tissue, and patches of reduced NADH activity. Electron microscopy confirmed minicores.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to consanguineous parents. He was born at 33 weeks' gestation, needed resuscitation for asphyxia, had a weak suck, and showed a congenital myopathic phenotype with elbow contractures and scoliosis from the first months of life. Motor development and intellect were normal. However, he developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, dysphagia, and respiratory involvement. The case report states that nocturnal noninvasive ventilation was needed from age 16 years, whereas the discussion of the same report states that respiratory support was needed from age 6. Serum creatine kinase, brain and spine MRI, ECG, and echocardiogram were normal. Nerve conduction was normal apart from reduced amplitude of the muscle evoked potential. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, preserved facial expression, cleft palate, global areflexia, and contractures of the elbows and ankles. He walked without support with an equinovarus-supinated foot stance, hyperlordosis, and pelvic tilt, and he later needed a manual wheelchair for longer distances. He underwent bilateral Achilles tendon tenotomy and vertebral arthrodesis. From age 17 years he had swallowing difficulties and recurrent aspiration pneumonias. A muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: fiber size variation, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed myofibrillar alterations, including whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) performed whole-genome sequencing in 1 affected member of a family with CMYO10B (family 1030) and filtered the variants using linkage data. In the 3 affected sibs they identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: C326R and C774R. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disorder in all 6 family members. Neither mutation was present in public variant databases or in 715 and 645 genotyped controls, respectively. Both affected cysteine residues lie in atypical EGF-like domains and are conserved in all 43 species examined. Boyden et al. (2012) also screened MEGF10 in 190 additional patients with unexplained myopathy. They found a single heterozygous R71W mutation in a patient with a similar phenotype (subject 105-1), inherited from an unaffected parent. No second mutation was identified, including by sequencing of muscle cDNA. Knockdown of megf10 in zebrafish supported pathogenicity.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) knocked down megf10 in zebrafish using 4 different splice-blocking morpholinos. The resulting morphants had unhatched eggs, curved or bent tails, impaired swimming, and reduced motility in response to touch. checks.evidence_quote: Sanger sequencing was also performed and confirmed that the patient was homozygous for the variant

checks.claim: Both parents of the 22-year-old Italian man were heterozygous carriers of the MEGF10 C699S mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: the patient was homozygous for the variant, and both parents were carriers

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S mutation was absent from ClinVar.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD)

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S mutation was absent from gnomAD.
checks.evidence_quote: This variant is absent in genomic databases (such as ClinVar and gnomAD)

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S mutation affects a conserved residue.
checks.evidence_quote: affects a conserved residue (GERP score = 5.85)

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S mutation was predicted to be damaging by in silico tools.
checks.evidence_quote: is predicted to be pathogenic by several in silico tools

checks.claim: The MEGF10 C699S mutation was classified as likely pathogenic under ACMG criteria.
checks.evidence_quote: This amino acid change is further classified as likely pathogenic according to the ACMG criteria (PM2, PP3).
